reason: The bone window has spaces awaiting mineral, so this directly addresses the bone-strengthening goal.
expectation: The mineral will strengthen the living bone framework.

alternatives.reason: The cells could also start building a muscle, but either goal is a reasonable place to begin.

effect: The mineral strengthened the living bones while leaving the joint free to move. Next I can build the muscles.
reaction: It was useful to see that the joint's soft tissues stayed unmineralized.
reason: The front attachments have a space for muscle cells, as the chapter describes.
expectation: The cells will form a muscle between the front tendon attachments.

alternatives.reason: I could build the muscle behind the elbow first instead.

effect: The front cells formed the biceps, which pulls to bend the elbow. The back attachment still needs a muscle.
reaction: The picture made the connection between the muscle's position and bending clear.
reason: The chapter says to place the same kind of muscle cells at the attachments behind the elbow too.
expectation: The cells will form a muscle behind the elbow that pulls in the opposite direction.

effect: The triceps completes the opposing muscle pair: its position behind the elbow lets it straighten the arm. All chapter goals are complete.
reaction: It was satisfying to see how the same kind of muscle cells can help move the elbow in opposite directions.

mostWorthwhile.text: Building the biceps and triceps was most worthwhile because their positions explain how pulling can bend or straighten the elbow.

leastWorthwhile.text: Adding the mineral was straightforward and less interesting than comparing the two muscles, although it showed why the joint stays movable.

surprise.text: I hadn't expected the same kind of muscle cells to produce opposite movements just because of where the muscles attach.

arbitrary.text: Nothing felt arbitrary; the spaces in the pictures and the goals gave each action a clear purpose.

continue.text: I would choose to continue if another chapter connects body parts to what they do as clearly as the elbow example did.
